item.title: Peter Pan, Puer Aeternus, and the Rejection of Adulthood
item.description:
Career

Peter Pan, Puer Aeternus, and the Rejection of Adulthood

Why is it so difficult for some to do what society says adults should do?

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Puer aeternus or puella aeterna is an archetypal pattern of behavior prominent in certain men and women.
  • The puer phenomenon is not a formal personality disorder.
  • The puer or puella syndrome can have both negative and positive effects on our lives.

Why do some people struggle with transitioning to adulthood while others do it seemingly effortlessly? What is adulthood, anyway? How do we define it as a society? And does becoming an "adult" mean having to forget about one's "inner child"?

The Puer Aeternus Personality

Most readers here will be familiar with the story of Peter Pan, or the Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up, published in 1904 by playwright James Matthew Barrie who novelized the play in his 1911 book Peter and Wendy. Some may have heard of the "Peter Pan syndrome" described in psychologist Dan Kiley's bestselling book The Peter Pan Syndrome: Men Who Have Never Grown Up (1983). But fewer may be aware of C.G. Jung's (1934) concepts of the puer aeternus and puella aeterna or the "eternal boy or girl."

Marie-Louise von Franz
Source: Wikimedia Commons

For Jung and his followers (see, for example, Swiss psychotherapist M.-L. von Franz's 1970 excellent book Puer Aeternus: A Psychological Study of the Adult Struggle with the Paradise of Childhood), the puer or puella are a type of man or woman who, despite chronological maturation, fiercely resist emotional maturation and the behaviors, responsibilities, commitments and other cultural expectations of so-called adulthood.

The Latin term puer aeternus originates from Ovid's Metamorphoses, referring to a "child-god" or divine or "eternal youth." Jung called it the "divine child," an archetypal figure representing potentiality, balance, and wholeness, a symbol of the Self. In this sense, the puer or puella is closely related to the popular contemporary concept of the "inner child" (see my prior post), and can be understood as the manifest conflict between the "adult self" and the "child self" within the personality, each part vying to express itself and striving to have its needs met in the world, something quite common in clinical practice and a key to therapeutic progress when recognized and properly addressed.

Is the Puella or Puer a Type of Personality Disorder?

Though not a formally recognized disorder by the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5-TR (2022), as with certain psychiatric diagnoses such as psychosis, psychopathy, or borderline personality, puer or puella are terms that tend to at times be used pejoratively by some clinicians when referring to patients who, in various ways, appear to be obstinately refusing or resisting growing up. The typical puer or puella personality is "resistant to commitment in work or relationships and unable to completely abandon the dreams and fantasies of adolescence" (1970) or of childhood. This pattern of behavior has also been described by Jung, Baynes, and von Franz as the "provisional life," meaning that, in most cases, no real roots are put down nor major commitments made so as to keep one's options open as much as possible to something better or more exciting or meaningful happening in the future.

Moreover, there is a general tendency to avoid tedium, hard work, and ordinariness, which prevents the puer or puella from pursuing and attaining what they truly want due to being unwilling to accept the boring and difficult task of actually achieving it. Hard, sustained, monotonous work is something they have no patience for. Such provisional behavior has been compared to a beautiful butterfly flitting endlessly from one flower to another, tasting the various sweet nectars rather than lighting on one for any significant length of time.

There is a strong avoidance of anything that would limit or curtail one's freedom and potentialities in life. This assiduous avoidance could consist of refusing to choose and fully commit to a profession or job, place to live such as a city, state, or country, purchasing (if financially feasible) or renting and remaining in a home or residence for any significant period of time, being relatively non-committal regarding marriage or other intimate relationships, etc. The secret here is that the puer or puella does not ever want to be pinned down (like a collected butterfly), bound, hindered, restrained, constricted, forced or limited by finitude, reality, tedium, ordinariness, or even death. They tend to be what are euphemistically called "free spirits."

Paradoxically, the puer or puella strives to exemplify the observation by Heraclitus that one can never step into the same stream twice but, at the same time, they cannot fully commit themselves to the moment. They cannot be firmly grounded and fully present in the here-and-now. Indeed, from a more existential perspective, the puer or puella can be seen as rebelling against the existential facts of finitude and mortality: If one refuses to grow up or get old, one cannot die. So this syndrome is fundamentally, and typically unconsciously, a denial of death and its inevitability.

And it entails also a protest against the loss or limitation of our protean nature toward transformation, change, and growth. (Proteus was in Greek mythology a prophetic water god who would constantly shift his shape to escape whenever caught, confronted or questioned.)

What happens when the essence of who we are and how we want to live does not comport with the preconceived image of adulthood held and promulgated by parents, peers, and society as a whole? There is a profound resistance in the puer and puella to subjectively define oneself or be objectively defined by others. The refusal to be pigeon-holed, categorized, labeled, or perceived as being just this or that, fish or fowl. Not wanting to be forced by society into some preconceived notion of adulthood and then being defined in that way. Clinging to the intrinsic capacity to recreate or reinvent ourselves at any time as we so desire, something that becomes more difficult to do as we grow older.

Who Defines Adulthood?

For instance, must every person marry or have children or some career to be considered an adult? What if this is not the kind of life they envision or wish to create for themselves? What if they choose to never marry, nor have children, nor commit to any particular career, job, or geographic location in which to reside? Does this really make someone neurotic and not an adult? Or might they just be a different type of adult? A non-conformist refusing to turn themselves and their lives into what society tells them to.

As Freud discusses in his classic text Civilization and its Discontents (1930), the implicit and explicit collective pressures of socialization can be experienced as stifling or suffocating the individual's instincts and natural way of being in the world, which results in feelings of discontent, frustration, resentment, and anger. From this perspective, it could be asked: Which is more mature and adult? To conform and submit to societal pressures and expectations regarding lifestyle and its consequences or to try to be true to oneself in finding and fulfilling one's personal destiny, whatever that may be, despite the collective disapproval and guilt feelings such uncompromising integrity, authenticity, and individuality engenders?

Of course, there are powerful, primal, archetypal, and primitive biological urges or instincts for procreation and perpetuation of the human race to consider that compel the individual toward reproduction and relationship during adolescence and beyond. But who ultimately decides what adulthood looks like? Does becoming an adult necessarily mean submitting or surrendering to such powerful instinctual drives? Or can one decide whether to do so not?

One example of such a choice is the deeply religious or spiritual person's decision to be celibate, meaning not to marry or have sex, as in, say the case of Catholic priests, nuns, or Buddhist monks like the Dalai Lama (see my prior post.) Are such people all puers or puellas? Perhaps, but this prejudicial perception fails to recognize and appreciate the healthy, positive, spiritual, creative aspects of the puer aeturnus or puella aeterna personality of which each of us partakes to some extent.

item.title: The Evolutionary Roots of the Male Mental Health Crisis
item.description:
Parenting

The Evolutionary Roots of the Male Mental Health Crisis

If we attempt to destroy traditional masculinity, what will emerge in its place?

Posted August 19, 2026

It’s striking how long men’s troubles have gone unnoticed. Men account for roughly 80% of suicides in the United States and nearly three out of every four “deaths of despair,” a term coined by economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton for the combination of deaths due to drug overdoses, alcohol-related deaths, and suicides (Case & Deaton, 2021; Reeves, 2022). And this pattern extends past mortality as well: Among Americans aged 25 to 34, 47% of women now hold a bachelor’s degree compared to 37% of men, a gap that did not exist as recently as 1995 (Pew Research Center, 2024), while the share of men ages 25 to 54 outside the labor force entirely has roughly doubled since the 1970s, rising from 5.8% to 11.4% (Bengali et al., 2023).

The consequences of men’s struggles affect everyone. For instance, when young men’s economic prospects collapse, marriage and fertility fall along with them, premature mortality rises, and a larger share of children end up in single-parent households below the poverty line (Autor et al., 2019). Unemployment is itself a documented cause of depression, and meta-analytic evidence across hundreds of studies finds the effect is stronger for men than for women (Paul & Moser, 2009). The downstream costs to those children are also well established, with the most rigorous designs continuing to find that father absence reduces high school graduation and harms social-emotional adjustment and adult mental health (McLanahan et al., 2013). Men who are struggling also make less reliable partners and less present fathers, and this places a further burden on women to pick up the slack. Thus, anyone invested in how women and girls are doing has a direct stake in men possessing a positive and healthy masculinity.

Unfortunately, there’s a strong social trend that sees masculinity itself as the problem (APA, 2018; Reeves, 2022), and it’s taboo in many parts of American society to talk about any area where men might have a relative strength. This leads to a portrayal of masculinity as essentially an all-bad category: full of negative traits and entirely lacking in positive qualities. And men who receive this message may feel that they need to choose between being bad and masculine (perhaps in the vein of Andrew Tate) or good and emasculated (perhaps anxious, inhibited, passive, guilty, weak, immature, or self-hating). In short, young men are increasingly struggling to find a sense of their masculinity that is authentic, useful, confident, assertive, valued, sustainable, and fulfilling.

How did we get here? In a recent article, clinician Yedidya Levy identifies three cultural shifts, arguing that each one has bumped up against features of evolved male psychology in ways that are making things worse for men.

How We Talk About Masculinity Now

The first shift Levy describes is how we talk about, and have come to view, masculine traits. Competitiveness, stoicism, and the desire to protect and provide are increasingly treated as “problematic” rather than capacities that could be channeled in useful directions. For instance, in 2018, the American Psychological Association published practice guidelines that classified “traditional masculinity ideology” as a clinical risk factor (APA, 2018). Of course, any trait (whether it’s deemed masculine or not) becomes a liability in the extreme, and indeed the same is true of feminine traits. But as practiced by most men most of the time, competitiveness, stoicism, and the drive to protect and provide are not pathologies. Instead of suppressing them, boys can be taught to channel these tendencies and thrive, becoming more useful and helpful members of society. To label the disposition itself defective, rather than its excesses, is to communicate to young men that the problem is not something they do but something they are. And a lot of them hear exactly that.

Missing Fathers, Missing Rituals

The second shift Levy identifies is demographic: About a quarter of American children now grow up without a father in the home. The research connecting father absence to higher rates of dropout, addiction, and premature death is extensive (Farrell & Gray, 2018). For a lot of boys, their father is the only working example they have of what it looks like when a man effectively manages frustration, takes responsibility for his behavior, and shows up even when he doesn’t feel like it.

And the third shift centers on the dissolution of tradition. At some point, Western society stopped marking the transition from boyhood to manhood. Nearly every pre-modern culture had some public ritual for this, and anthropologists have long noted that the ritual itself was never really the main event (van Gennep, 1960). Instead, what mattered was the announcement: the community telling boys they had crossed a significant threshold, that their community had noticed, and that there was now an important role waiting for them in a society where people counted on them. As society has become increasingly prosperous, we abandoned those rites and never replaced them with anything analogous.

Why These Changes Affect Men So Hard

For most of human history, a man’s standing in his group depended on what he could contribute, whether that be through demonstrating his competence or defending against threats. Among contemporary hunter-horticulturalists, for example, men earn standing both through their skill, knowledge, and generosity as well as through their dominance in physical contests (von Rueden et al., 2011). Yet this mindset is often the very same one now labeled “toxic.”

To the extent the mental health field has helped create an environment in which men feel their core traits are considered defects, then it also bears some responsibility for the consequences. Levy suggests that for clinicians, the most practical way to begin remedying this situation is to make sure that men who need help can walk through the door without expecting to be told, once again, that they are the problem. If any of this deserves the word toxic, it may be telling a generation of boys that who they are is wrong. Perhaps the remedy starts with telling them the opposite.

item.title: Identity Lag: Why Self-Image Updates Slower Than Your Résumé
item.description:
Imposter Syndrome

Identity Lag: Why Self-Image Updates Slower Than Your Résumé

Impostor feelings may not be a confidence problem. They may be a timing problem.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Impostor feelings may be a timing problem. Your self-model updates slower than your title.
  • Each promotion resets your peer group, so identity lag scales with success rather than resolving.
  • Impostor thoughts aren't permanent; research shows they fade as people become established in a new role.
  • Organizations budget 6–18 months for senior transitions. Your self-concept isn't behind schedule.

Not long ago, I was invited to speak to a room of MIT Sloan fellows about building with your brain. We talked about founder mindset, cognition, and how identity holds up under the pressure of building something. The room was full of C-suite executives, founders, and experts in their respective fields — people whose accomplishments were not in any reasonable dispute.

I will admit that I felt a flicker on the way in: These people run companies. I am here to tell them something they don't know?

Source: Christina @ wocintechchat.com / Unsplash

Then we got to the questions, and what surprised me was that the questions weren’t about strategy or scaling or hiring. Over and over, in different phrasings, the room asked a version of the same thing: Why do I still feel like a fraud? Where does this come from? What do I do about it?

It was a roomful of people at the top of their fields, privately auditing their right to be in the room (including myself!).

I have thought about that afternoon a lot since, because the explanation that impostor syndrome is a confidence deficit doesn't fit what I saw. Those people weren't short on confidence. They were running on outdated information about themselves.

The self-model updates conservatively. Your title doesn't

Here is a distinction I have come to call identity lag: the gap between how fast your external status changes and how fast your internal self-model can revise to match it.

Your sense of who you are isn't a feeling. It's a model, assembled from years of accumulated evidence, and it updates the way any well-built model updates: conservatively, and in proportion to how much new data it receives. Psychologist William Swann's research on self-verification has shown for decades that people actively seek out feedback confirming their existing self-views, and resist information that outpaces them, even when that information is flattering. This sounds counterintuitive, but it’s our brain’s way of trying to stay coherent.

The unnerving part is that resistance to updating is strongest in people who are most certain of their self-concept. That is to say, the more clearly you know who you are, the slower that picture revises.

Meanwhile, your résumé changes in an afternoon. Someone sends an email, and by lunch you have a new title, a new salary band, and a new set of people who expect you to have opinions. Yet inside, you're still the same person who came to work that day.

Why success makes it worse instead of better

There's a second mechanism, and it's the one that explains why this doesn't resolve as you advance.

When you get promoted, your reference group is replaced overnight. You get a new room and new peers, and they have been in that room longer than you have. Your self-model is still catching up to your last achievement.

This is why identity lag scales with accomplishment rather than dissolving. Every advancement resets the peer group faster than the self-model can absorb the previous one. Success doesn't cure the uncomfortable feeling, it re-triggers it, which is precisely why a room of MIT fellows had more of it, not less.

The part where the lag is doing something useful

MIT's Basima Tewfik has spent years revisiting this phenomenon, and her findings complicate the standard story in a useful direction. Across four studies of more than 3,600 people, employees who more frequently had impostor thoughts at work were rated by others as more interpersonally effective, because those thoughts pushed them into a more other-focused orientation. They listened harder.

Additionally, she found no cost to performance, and she found the thoughts weren't permanent: People shed them as they became more established.

Despite that lag being uncomfortable, it is the thing keeping you curious and coachable during the exact period when overconfidence would cost you most. Confidence earns respect; overconfidence paired with an inability to hear feedback ends careers. The lag is, temporarily, holding you on the right side of that line.

What actually updates the model

The self-model revises based on evidence, and evidence requires repetitions, which requires time in the role. Herminia Ibarra's research on professional transitions describes it as experimenting with provisional selves: trying the new identity on, in public, imperfectly, and letting the results accumulate.

This raises the question everyone actually wants answered: how long will this go on?

No one has measured it, because no one has been studying this as a timing problem. But we have a useful proxy. Organizations already know that senior transitions take six to eighteen months to complete. McKinsey's data shows most new executives need well beyond ninety days to reach full speed, and stakeholders give incoming CEOs roughly nine months to form a vision and over a year to build a team.

So here is the reframe I'd offer to that room: Your organization has already budgeted a year or more for you to become the person your title says you are. Your self-concept is working on the same schedule.

You are not behind. You are on time.

item.title: The Link Between Self-Mistrust and Adult ADHD
item.description:
ADHD

The Link Between Self-Mistrust and Adult ADHD

Why do so many adults with ADHD find it hard to trust themselves?

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Self-mistrust beliefs have been proposed as a core thinking theme in adults with ADHD.
  • The nature of adult ADHD increases procrastination and other matters that erode self-trust.
  • Some recent studies lend credence to the association of self-mistrust and ADHD, though indirectly.
  • Insights from these studies strengthen a focus on building self-trust combined with coping skills for ADHD.

Mistrust beliefs are typically other-focused, rooted in one's experiences of having been wronged, abandoned, or abused by others in trusted relationships. These experiences leave them wary and on guard about others’ motives.

Does adult ADHD leave you feeling you cannot trust yourself? Read this for some new insights.
Source: Brett Jordan/Pexels

Self-Mistrust and Adult ADHD

My first book on cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for adult ADHD,1 is where I first made mention of “self-mistrust” beliefs. They became apparent to me in countless sessions hearing clients’ self-doubts and corresponding self-recriminations and frustrations with themselves for consistently not doing what they know they needed to do and that they knew full well they could do.

But the insidiousness of the effects of ADHD is that they were still unable to reliably count on themselves to implement intentions as a consequence. The consistent inconsistency of ADHD left them believing, and often saying aloud, “I can’t trust myself.”

Several years later, I stumbled across Albert Bandura’s construct of self-regulatory efficacy (SRE) while I was writing a book in which I took a stab at proposing a cognitive theme germane to adult ADHD.2 SRE’s description, that of a kind of meta-efficacy, fit with the consensus that ADHD is not a knowledge problem but a performance problem, self-dysregulation regularly punctuating the engagement and follow through on otherwise reasonable endeavors. Quoting Bandura:3

“In many spheres of functioning, people know full well how to perform the needed behavior. Here, the relevant efficacy beliefs concern self-regulatory capabilities—can people get themselves to stick with the behavior given the many dissuading conditions they will encounter? ... (T)hose who distrust their capacities to surmount unpleasant factors have little reason to put themselves through misery. In familiar activities that must be performed regularly to achieve desired results, it is perceived self-regulatory efficacy, rather than perceived efficacy for the activity per se, that is most relevant.” (p. 64, emphasis added)

Although I continue to propose such self-mistrust as a chief cognitive theme in adult ADHD,4 I present it as a hypothesis to be tested. When trying to find support for this idea in the literature, I typically only encounter SRE in research on matters like exercise adherence.

Self-Regulatory Efficacy and Protecting Against Procrastination

That is, until recently. Let me be clear from the outset that the two studies I stumbled upon did not include adults with ADHD. However, the studies addressed self-regulatory efficacy and its relationship to academic procrastination in college students. Procrastination for me is the top problem shared by most adults with ADHD, so the studies captured my interest.

The first study5 used general self-efficacy (SE) and self-regulatory efficacy (SRE) ratings as predictors of procrastination ratings and objective academic procrastination (measured with student-generated intended assignments and number of days needed to complete them) in a sample of 105 college students. SRE was associated with significantly less procrastination when compared with general SE, which would support the idea of self-trust. A conjecture for this surprising finding was that those with high general SE but low SRE may have been overconfident and thereby underestimated academic task difficulties.

The second study6 included a measure of visual imagery (a variable hypothesized to increase motivation and thereby reduce procrastination) to assess its relationship to SE, SRE, and procrastination behavior ratings in a sample of 148 college students. Again, SRE emerged as protecting against procrastination, especially for participants scoring high on visual imagery.

Oddly, when including visual imagery in an analysis of the most significant factors predicting procrastination, visual imagery was associated with more academic procrastination—except for those with high SRE! Again, self-trust in one’s efficacy increased ratings on one's ability to start and follow through on academic tasks.

Take Away Message for Adult ADHD

Such studies conducted with adults with ADHD would provide a clearer connection between self-mistrust, ADHD, and procrastination. But at least there is a connection between self-trust/SRE and less procrastination. Even these preliminary findings offer further justification for fostering self-trust armed with personalized, adapted skills for coping with adult ADHD.

item.title: Consciousness Leaves a Paper Trail
item.description:
Philosophy

Consciousness Leaves a Paper Trail

What if our puzzlement about consciousness is itself a clue?

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • The hard problem asks why neural processing is accompanied by subjective experience.
  • Causal closure leaves no obvious room for consciousness to influence physical events.
  • If experience causes nothing, physicalism must explain why we keep talking about it.
  • Our bafflement about qualia may itself be caused by consciousness.

Consciousness might be the one fact we know too intimately to understand fully. Whenever we encounter ourselves or a world, consciousness is already there, supplying the first-person dimension.

This brings us to David Chalmers’ “hard problem” of consciousness. Science can investigate how brains discriminate stimuli, direct attention, form memories, and produce reports. These are difficult problems, but we know what sort of explanation we seek: mechanisms performing functions. The hard problem is more fundamental. Why should experience accompany those functions? (Chalmers, 1995, 1996; Levine, 1983).

Philosophers call these subjective qualities qualia: the redness of red, the bitterness of coffee, the painfulness of pain. A quale is not the brain’s ability to distinguish red from green or pain from touch, but the subjective character accompanying that ability (Nagel, 1974; Jackson, 1982). It is unusual, to say the least; but the question is also whether this phenomenal ingredient merely accompanies physical processing or makes a causal difference.

A Physicist’s Uncomfortable Argument

My friend and colleague Avshalom Elitzur, renowned quantum physicist and brilliant philosopher, has developed one of the most ingenious contemporary arguments in this territory. These questions also formed the subject of two volumes that Avshalom and I edited together, Mind and Its Place in the World and Irreducibly Conscious (Batthyany and Elitzur, 2006, 2009). His own argument leads towards the unsettling possibility that the current physical description is radically incomplete. For a time, this made him a reluctant dualist. From what I now hear, he has recently drifted towards the equally wild, and rather beautiful, territory of panpsychism—still hardly safe ground for a physicist.

The Price of Letting Consciousness Act

His “Bafflement Argument” gains its bite from the causal closure of the physical world: every physical event has a sufficient physical cause. Neurons fire because of prior physical conditions; muscles contract because neurons fire. Physics should tell the entire causal story without a blank space marked “mind intervenes here” (Kim, 1998).

This is a load-bearing commitment of modern science. If consciousness alters a neural event, its physical account is incomplete—and that carries a penalty. On Elitzur’s analysis, allowing nonphysical consciousness to influence the brain may require revisiting conservation laws or thermodynamics. A mental influence cannot be slipped into the equations without paying for it somewhere.

The usual escape is to declare consciousness causally idle. One may identify qualia with brain activity, or regard them as real but epiphenomenal: the brain produces consciousness, while consciousness produces nothing in return. Qualia add nothing to behaviour. Elitzur calls this the “Qualia Inaction Postulate.”

The Clue Consciousness Wasn’t Supposed to Leave

Here comes his decisive move. Instead of treating qualia only as objects in need of explanation, Elitzur draws attention to a further physical fact: human beings are baffled by them (Elitzur, 1989, 2009).

We notice that their felt character seems absent from physical description. We formulate the explanatory gap, invent philosophical zombies, write books and organize conferences. Bafflement acquires a physical footprint.

Elitzur’s argument is therefore almost embarrassingly direct: we are baffled by qualia because we have qualia. If experience explains our talking about experience, then experience has affected physical behaviour. Consciousness has touched the controls after all.

Can Bafflement Be Explained Away?

The physicalist can reply that the brain constructs an incomplete model of its own operations and mistakes that incompleteness. Bafflement would then be a metacognitive illusion generated entirely by neural machinery—an approach developed more generally by contemporary illusionists (Frankish, 2016).

That is possible, but not yet an explanation. If bafflement is an error (qua physicalism), there must be a physical or computational account of it. The physicalist must explain why information processing makes a system insist that it possesses an unobservable phenomenal ingredient. Such an account might reveal the hard problem as a defect of intelligent self-representation. Until then, “illusion” labels the problem rather than solving it.

The Zombie Who Writes About Consciousness

Elitzur presses the point through Chalmers’ philosophical zombie: our perfect physical duplicate, but without experience. Chalmers accepts that his zombie twin would nevertheless write the same books, love the same deep greens and purples, and complain that physics leaves qualia out (Chalmers, 1996).

But in a certain way, this is the strangest part. Why should a being without experience independently discover an explanatory gap about experience? It may report access to internal states but ignorance of their machinery. That concerns information and self-monitoring—an “easy” problem—not why any state should feel like anything.

This difference drives Elitzur’s “Asymmetry Proof.” The zombie’s perceptual states arise by physical necessity from its architecture; it cannot subtract them while holding every physical fact constant. Chalmers, however, claims that he can subtract qualia while leaving every physical and functional fact untouched. The two forms of bafflement therefore have different objects: incomplete access to processing versus the apparent possibility of all that processing occurring with nobody home. Explaining the first does not explain the second (Bailey, 2006).

Something Has to Give

The bafflement argument exposes the tension among four attractive claims: qualia are real; they are not reducible to functions; the physical domain is causally closed; and our reports about experience are genuinely responsive to the experiences they report. Retaining all four makes our discourse about consciousness look like an extraordinary coincidence.

Elitzur accepts the penalty and loosens causal closure. Others may deny qualia, reduce them to functional self-models, or insist that our reports would be identical in an entirely experience-free world. But each position now owes an argument. The bafflement argument prevents the causal impotence of consciousness from being treated as a quiet, cost-free compromise.

It is simple, elegant and, in the age of artificial intelligence, possibly programmatic. Above all, it remains a standing challenge to the other side. If consciousness makes no causal difference, why has it left the physical world so full of arguments about consciousness?

Any takers?
